category: Launching, Environment, Licensing, File Formats & Device Families
description: Everything around the tool rather than inside a design: the vivado command line and startup scripts, settings64, version, cs_server, environment variables (XILINX_VIVADO, license variables, XILINX_LOCAL_USER_DATA, XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO, XILINX_PATH), the installation and per-user configuration directories, licensing mechanics, journal/log and crash files, the project and run directory structure, the main file formats (.xpr, .xdc, .dcp, .xci/.xcix, .bd, .hwh, .xsa and legacy .hdf/.dsa, EDIF, SDF, SAIF/VCD, .mmi/.mem/.elf, .coe/.mif, CSV pin files, IBIS, UCF, .nky) and AMD device families and part-name decoding.

tools.name: vivado command-line options (vivado -help)
tools.description: Full option set of the vivado launcher: -mode gui|tcl|batch selects IDE, interactive Tcl shell or run-and-exit; -source runs a script at startup; -journal/-log rename (and -appjournal/-applog append to) the session transcripts while -nojournal/-nolog disable them; -tempDir relocates temporary files; -tclargs passes the remaining words to the script's argv; a trailing .xpr or .dcp is opened on startup; -version prints the release and exits. The loader also accepts -stack <size> to enlarge the stack for crashes caused by deep recursion in synthesis (AR 64434).
tools.usage: vivado [-mode gui|tcl|batch] [-init] [-source <file.tcl>] [-nojournal] [-appjournal] [-journal <file.jou>] [-nolog] [-applog] [-log <file.log>] [-version] [-tclargs <args...>] [-tempDir <dir>] [-robot <jar>] [-verbose] [-stack <size>] [<project.xpr | design.dcp>]

parameters.name: -mode
parameters.description: gui (default), tcl (interactive shell, no GUI) or batch (run -source script, then exit).

parameters.name: -init
parameters.description: Source the vivado.tcl initialisation file.

parameters.name: -journal / -log
parameters.description: Names of the journal (default vivado.jou) and log (default vivado.log) files in the launch directory.

parameters.name: -appjournal / -applog
parameters.description: Open the journal/log in append mode instead of rotating the previous one into a backup file.

parameters.name: -tempDir
parameters.description: Directory for temporary files - useful on shared build machines with a small /tmp.

parameters.name: -tclargs
parameters.description: Everything after it is passed to the script in $argc/$argv; it must be the last Vivado option.

parameters.name: <project>
parameters.description: An .xpr to open, or a .dcp checkpoint (e.g. vivado design.dcp -source report.tcl).

parameters.name: -stack
parameters.description: Loader option (not listed by -help) to increase the process stack size, e.g. -stack 2000, used as a workaround for stack-overflow segmentation faults.

tools.example:
vivado -version
vivado -mode tcl -nojournal -log shell.log
vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl -journal build.jou -log build.log -tempDir /scratch/vtmp -tclargs --part xczu9eg-ffvb1156-2-e --top top
vivado ./impl_1/top_routed.dcp -source ./scripts/reports.tcl
tools.notes: Run vivado -help on the installed release for the authoritative list; options can change between versions. On Windows the launcher is vivado.bat, so call it with 'call vivado ...' inside other batch files or control will not return. See also the existing 'vivado -mode batch -source' entry for CI exit-status handling.

tools.name: settings64.sh / settings64.bat
tools.description: Environment setup scripts shipped in each tool's installation directory that put the tool's bin directory on PATH and set XILINX_VIVADO (or XILINX_VITIS / XILINX_HLS for those tools) and the library paths the executables need. Sourcing them is required before calling vivado, xsim, xelab, hw_server, bootgen, updatemem and friends from a plain shell, CI job or Makefile.
tools.usage:
Linux (bash):  source <install>/Vivado/<version>/settings64.sh      (csh: settings64.csh)
Windows (cmd): call <install>\Vivado\<version>\settings64.bat
2025.1 and later layout: <install>/<version>/Vivado/settings64.sh

parameters.name: settings64.csh
parameters.description: C-shell variant for csh/tcsh users.

parameters.name: Tool-specific scripts
parameters.description: Vitis, Vitis HLS and Vivado Lab have their own settings64 scripts; sourcing Vitis's usually also brings in the matching Vivado.

tools.example:
# Linux CI step
source /tools/Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2/settings64.sh
echo $XILINX_VIVADO
vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl

:: Windows batch file
call C:\Xilinx\Vivado\2024.2\settings64.bat
call vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl
tools.notes: Sourcing two different versions in one shell mixes PATH entries - start a fresh shell per version. Starting with 2025.1 the default folder structure changed from <install>/Vivado/<version> to <install>/<version>/Vivado, so hard-coded paths in scripts need updating when moving to 2025.x.

tools.name: Vivado_init.tcl (startup script; xsim_init.tcl, vivado_lab_init.tcl)
tools.description: Tcl script sourced automatically every time Vivado starts, used to define team procs, set_param defaults, message rules, custom GUI buttons or board repository paths. It is searched in the installation (<install>/Vivado/<version>/scripts/Vivado_init.tcl, for a site-wide script), then the version-specific user directory, then the version-independent user directory; the naming convention <program>_init.tcl also gives xsim_init.tcl and vivado_lab_init.tcl.
tools.usage:
1. <install>/Vivado/<version>/scripts/Vivado_init.tcl
2. Windows %APPDATA%/Xilinx/Vivado/<version>/Vivado_init.tcl | Linux $HOME/.Xilinx/Vivado/<version>/Vivado_init.tcl
3. Windows %APPDATA%/Xilinx/Vivado/Vivado_init.tcl | Linux $HOME/.Xilinx/Vivado/Vivado_init.tcl

parameters.name: init.tcl
parameters.description: Pre-2017.1 name; still sourced (with a deprecation message) if Vivado_init.tcl does not exist.

parameters.name: Installation copy
parameters.description: Lets a company or group give every user the same initialisation; user copies add to or override it.

tools.example:
# ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/Vivado_init.tcl
set_param general.maxThreads 8
set_param board.repoPaths [list /opt/boards/XilinxBoardStore/boards]
set_param tclapp.enableGitAccess 0
set_msg_config -id {Synth 8-327} -new_severity ERROR   ;# inferred latches fail the build
if {[file exists /opt/team/procs.tcl]} { source /opt/team/procs.tcl }
tools.notes: Keep init scripts quiet and fast - they also run for batch builds, so anything they set silently changes CI results. Settings in an init script are invisible to someone reproducing the build elsewhere; prefer putting build-relevant parameters in the build script itself.

tools.name: version
tools.description: Returns the Vivado release, build number and build date of the running tool; with -short it returns only the release number (e.g. 2024.2). Build scripts use it to refuse to run on the wrong release, since checkpoints, IP and block designs are release-specific.
tools.usage: version [-short] [-quiet] [-verbose]

parameters.name: -short
parameters.description: Return just the version number string.

tools.notes: From the shell, vivado -version prints the same information without starting a session. report_environment gives the full environment for bug reports.

tools.name: cs_server
tools.description: ChipScope server: the debug-core communication server used for Versal devices, sitting next to hw_server. hw_server handles JTAG, programming and memory access, while cs_server handles higher-level debug cores (ILA, VIO, IBERT/transceiver and memory-calibration debug on Versal); the ChipScoPy Python API and Vivado's Hardware Manager connect to both. Its default URL is TCP:localhost:3042 (hw_server TCP:localhost:3121).
tools.usage:
Started automatically by Vivado when the default URL is used; manual start from the tools' bin directory: cs_server
Vivado: connect_hw_server -url <host>:3121 -cs_url <host>:3042
ChipScoPy: create_session(hw_server_url="TCP:<host>:3121", cs_server_url="TCP:<host>:3042")

parameters.name: -cs_url (connect_hw_server)
parameters.description: URL of the cs_server to use; if the default URL is given and none is running, Vivado launches one.

parameters.name: Version matching
parameters.description: cs_server, hw_server and ChipScoPy should all be the same release.

tools.example:
# Remote Versal board: both servers run on the lab PC 'labpc'
open_hw_manager
connect_hw_server -url labpc:3121 -cs_url labpc:3042
open_hw_target
# Python
# from chipscopy import create_session
# s = create_session(hw_server_url="TCP:labpc:3121", cs_server_url="TCP:labpc:3042")
tools.notes: Not needed for 7 series / UltraScale(+) debug, which go through hw_server only. Firewalls must allow both ports for remote debug.

tools.name: XILINX_VIVADO / XILINX_VITIS / XILINX_HLS
tools.description: Environment variables holding the installation root of each tool: XILINX_VIVADO (set by Vivado's settings64 script and by the launcher itself), XILINX_VITIS for Vitis and XILINX_HLS for Vitis HLS. Scripts and Makefiles use them to locate executables, simulation libraries, board files and example data without hard-coding the version path.
tools.usage:
Tcl: $::env(XILINX_VIVADO)
bash: $XILINX_VIVADO   |  cmd: %XILINX_VIVADO%

parameters.name: XILINX_VIVADO
parameters.description: e.g. /tools/Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2 or C:/Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2 (2025.1+: <install>/2025.1/Vivado).

parameters.name: XILINX_VITIS / XILINX_HLS
parameters.description: Set by the Vitis and Vitis HLS settings64 scripts; v++ and vitis_hls rely on them.

tools.example:
puts "Running from $::env(XILINX_VIVADO)"
set boards [file join $::env(XILINX_VIVADO) data boards board_files]
puts [glob -nocomplain -directory $boards *]
# Makefile
# XSIM_LIB := $(XILINX_VIVADO)/data/xsim
tools.notes: Do not set XILINX_VIVADO by hand to a different release than the vivado on PATH; tools then load mismatched libraries. XILINX_XRT (set by the XRT setup script) is the runtime counterpart used by Vitis acceleration hosts.

tools.name: XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE / LM_LICENSE_FILE
tools.description: License search-path variables read by the FlexNet-based licensing in Vivado and Vitis: each holds a list of license files, directories and/or <port>@<server> entries. AMD recommends XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE (named after the xilinxd vendor daemon); LM_LICENSE_FILE also works but is mainly for non-AMD or legacy paths.
tools.usage:
Linux:   export XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE=2100@licserver1:2100@licserver2:/home/me/.Xilinx/Xilinx.lic
Windows: set XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE=2100@licserver1;C:\licenses\Xilinx.lic
(or Vivado License Manager > Manage License Search Paths on Windows)

parameters.name: <port>@<server>
parameters.description: Floating license server; AMD's default port is 2100.

parameters.name: Separators
parameters.description: ':' on Linux, ';' on Windows between entries.

parameters.name: Default locations
parameters.description: Without the variable, the tools also search the per-user license directory (%APPDATA%\XilinxLicense on Windows, ~/.Xilinx on Linux).

tools.example:
export XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE=2100@lic.example.com
vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl
# In Tcl, check what the session sees
puts $::env(XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE)
report_environment -file env.txt
tools.notes: On Linux the Vivado License Manager shows these fields read-only; set them in the shell profile or CI environment. Triad (three-server) configurations are listed as three port@host entries.

tools.name: XILINX_LOCAL_USER_DATA
tools.description: Controls whether Vivado caches data in the local user data area (~/.Xilinx on Linux, %APPDATA%\Xilinx on Windows). Setting it to NO stops Vivado from caching Tcl Store catalog files there, which the Xilinx Tcl Store developer workflow requires when testing apps from a local repository together with XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO.
tools.usage:
export XILINX_LOCAL_USER_DATA=NO      (Linux)
set XILINX_LOCAL_USER_DATA=NO         (Windows)
tools.example:
export XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO=$HOME/work/XilinxTclStore
export XILINX_LOCAL_USER_DATA=NO
vivado -mode tcl
# Vivado% tclapp::install mycompany::myapp
tools.notes: Only documented in the Tcl Store contributor guidance; behaviour beyond Tcl Store caching is not specified by AMD, so do not rely on it to make Vivado write nothing to the home directory.

tools.name: XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO
tools.description: Points Vivado at a local clone of the Xilinx Tcl Store instead of the public GitHub repository. Vivado adds the location to the Tcl auto_load path, which lets companies share a private app repository or developers test new apps before publishing; the catalog cannot be refreshed while it is set.
tools.usage:
Linux:   export XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO=<path>/XilinxTclStore   (csh: setenv XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO <path>)
Windows: set XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO=<path>\XilinxTclStore
tools.example:
git clone https://github.com/Xilinx/XilinxTclStore.git /opt/tclstore
export XILINX_TCLAPP_REPO=/opt/tclstore
vivado -mode tcl
# Vivado% tclapp::install xilinx::designutils
tools.notes: Combine with set_param tclapp.enableGitAccess 0 in Vivado_init.tcl for sites that forbid tools from contacting GitHub.

tools.name: XILINX_PATH (tactical patches)
tools.description: Environment variable used to apply an AMD tactical patch (distributed with an Answer Record) from a directory outside the installation: Vivado looks in XILINX_PATH before its own installation, so patched files override the originals without modifying the install. The alternative is extracting the patch into <install>/Vivado/<version>/patches/AR<number>.
tools.usage:
Linux:   export XILINX_PATH=/opt/patches/vivado-patch-AR<nnnnn>/vivado
Windows: set XILINX_PATH=C:\patches\vivado-patch-AR<nnnnn>\vivado\
Then run Vivado from the original installation.
tools.example:
unzip AR<nnnnn>_patch.zip -d /opt/patches/AR<nnnnn>
export XILINX_PATH=/opt/patches/AR<nnnnn>/vivado
vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl
# verify the fix as described in the Answer Record
tools.notes: Patches are release-specific; a stale XILINX_PATH left in a profile silently patches (or breaks) a different release. Prefer the in-install patches/ directory on shared build servers so every user gets the same fix.

tools.name: Vivado user configuration directory (%APPDATA%\Xilinx\Vivado\<version>, ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/<version>)
tools.description: Per-user, per-release directory where the IDE keeps its preferences and user-created assets: vivado.xml (Tools > Settings values), layouts/*.layout, themes/*.patheme, shortcuts/shortcuts.xml, commands/commands.paini (custom commands), strategies/ and reportstrategies/ (user strategies), the Vivado Store download area (xhub/board_store), the text-editor syntax-check cache and optional Vivado_init.tcl. Deleting or renaming it resets the IDE to factory defaults for that release.
tools.usage:
Windows: %APPDATA%\Xilinx\Vivado\<version>\   (plus %APPDATA%\Xilinx\Vivado\ for version-independent Vivado_init.tcl)
Linux:   ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/<version>/   (plus ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/)

parameters.name: vivado.xml
parameters.description: Written on exit with display colours, recent lists and other Tool Settings.

parameters.name: strategies / reportstrategies
parameters.description: User-defined run and report strategies created in Tools > Settings > Strategies.

parameters.name: xhub/board_store
parameters.description: Default location of board files and example designs installed from the Vivado Store.

tools.example:
# Reset a corrupted GUI state for 2024.2 (Linux) while keeping a backup
mv ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2 ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2.bak
vivado &
# Share custom strategies with a colleague
cp -r ~/.Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2/strategies /shared/team_strategies_2024.2
tools.notes: When started from the Windows Start menu, vivado.jou/vivado.log also land in %APPDATA%\Xilinx\Vivado. The directory layout inside the user profile did not change with the 2025.1 installation-directory restructuring.

tools.name: Vivado installation directory layout
tools.description: Where things live in an installation: bin/ (vivado, xvlog, xvhdl, xelab, xsim, hw_server, updatemem and other executables), lib/, data/ (device data, IP repository data/ip, board files data/boards/board_files, precompiled simulation libraries under data/xsim), scripts/ (site-wide Vivado_init.tcl), tps/ (third-party components), patches/ (tactical patches) and the settings64 scripts. Up to 2024.2 each tool installs as <install>/<Tool>/<version>; from 2025.1 the structure is <install>/<version>/<Tool>, with some shared folders moved up beside the tools.
tools.usage:
<= 2024.2:  <install>/Vivado/<version>/{bin,data,lib,scripts,tps,patches,settings64.*}
>= 2025.1:  <install>/<version>/Vivado/{bin,data,lib,scripts,...}
Default <install>: C:/Xilinx on Windows, /tools/Xilinx on Linux (chosen in the installer).
tools.example:
ls $XILINX_VIVADO/bin | grep -E '^(vivado|xelab|xsim|xvlog|hw_server|updatemem)$'
ls $XILINX_VIVADO/data/boards/board_files
# Add a missing device family later: Help > Add Design Tools or Devices
tools.notes: Never edit files under data/ip or data/boards in place - use your own ip_repo_paths and board.repoPaths so upgrades do not wipe the changes. On Windows avoid paths with spaces for the install root and project directories.

tools.name: Node-locked and floating licenses (FlexNet lmgrd / xilinxd, port 2100)
tools.description: AMD tool and IP licenses are FlexNet certificate files (.lic) generated on the AMD Product Licensing site. A node-locked license is one seat bound to a host ID (MAC address, disk serial or USB dongle) and is loaded locally; a floating license lives on a license server running lmgrd with the xilinxd vendor daemon and is checked out by clients over the network, limited to the purchased seat count. Server and client (node-locked) licenses cannot be mixed in one file.
tools.usage:
Server:  lmgrd -c <path>/Xilinx.lic -l <path>/lmgrd.log    (Linux: <tools>/lnx64.o/lmgrd; Windows: lmgrd.exe)
Client:  XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE=2100@<server>
Check:   lmutil lmstat -a -c 2100@<server>

parameters.name: Host ID
parameters.description: Identifier the license is locked to; easiest obtained by running the Vivado License Manager on the target machine.

parameters.name: Triad
parameters.description: Three redundant license servers; licensing continues while two are up.

parameters.name: Rehost / Delete
parameters.description: Done on the licensing site; the old .lic must then be destroyed (affidavit of destruction).

tools.example:
# License server (Linux)
/opt/xilinx_lic/lnx64.o/lmgrd -c /opt/xilinx_lic/Xilinx.lic -l /var/log/xilinx_lmgrd.log
# Client
export XILINXD_LICENSE_FILE=2100@licsrv
lmutil lmstat -a -c 2100@licsrv
tools.notes: Use the FlexNet utilities version required by the tool release (UG973 lists it); old lmgrd versions reject new certificates. Vivado ML Standard Edition, Lab Edition, hw_server and Kria/Alveo targets need no license; Enterprise-only devices and licensed IP do.

tools.name: vivado.jou / vivado.log (journal and log files)
tools.description: Every Vivado session writes a journal (vivado.jou: only the Tcl commands executed, including those echoed by GUI actions) and a log (vivado.log: commands plus all messages and results) into the launch directory. At the next launch the previous pair is kept as vivado_<id>.backup.jou / vivado_<id>.backup.log, and each design run writes its own vivado.jou/runme.log inside its run directory.
tools.usage: Location: the launch directory (Windows Start-menu launches: %APPDATA%\Xilinx\Vivado). Rename with vivado -journal/-log, append with -appjournal/-applog, disable with -nojournal/-nolog. GUI: File > Project > Open Journal File | Open Log File.
tools.example:
vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl -journal logs/build_$(date +%Y%m%d).jou -log logs/build_$(date +%Y%m%d).log
grep -E '^(ERROR|CRITICAL WARNING)' logs/build_*.log
# In the Tcl Console a comment is recorded in the journal but not executed:
# checkpoint before floorplan experiments
tools.notes: The journal is a starting point for scripts, not a script itself: it records GUI actions that may not replay cleanly and omits some actions. Launch Vivado from a per-project directory (or double-click the .xpr) so journals and logs do not pile up in the home directory.

tools.name: hs_err_pid<id>.log / vivado_pid<id>.str / vivado_pid<id>.debug / vivado_pid<id>.zip (crash files)
tools.description: Files written when Vivado hits an internal exception or crashes: hs_err_pid<id>.log (Java VM/native crash report), vivado_pid<id>.debug (error log), vivado_pid<id>.str (steps to reproduce - the GUI actions taken before the failure) and vivado_pid<id>.zip (an archive of these for support). They contain no design data and are what AMD support asks for together with vivado.jou and vivado.log.
tools.usage: Written to the launch directory. Attach vivado_pid<id>.zip to a support case, or if absent: vivado.jou, vivado.log, vivado_pid<id>.debug, hs_err_pid<id>.log and vivado_pid<id>.str.
tools.example:
ls -t hs_err_pid*.log vivado_pid* | head
# Also capture the environment for the report
echo 'report_environment -file env.txt' > env.tcl
vivado -mode batch -nojournal -nolog -source env.tcl
tools.notes: Repeated crashes in synthesis on large designs are often memory or stack related: check free RAM, reduce general.maxThreads, or try the -stack launcher option before filing a case.

tools.name: .xpr (project file) and project directory structure
tools.description: The .xpr is the XML project file created by create_project / the New Project wizard; it records part/board, filesets and their files (with project-relative paths), run definitions and strategies, and project settings. Beside it Vivado maintains <name>.srcs (sources and constraints by fileset), <name>.gen (IP/BD output products, 2020.2+ layout), <name>.runs (synthesis/implementation run directories), <name>.sim (simulation runs), <name>.cache (IP cache and tool caches), <name>.hw (Hardware Manager state) and <name>.ip_user_files (IP simulation/instantiation files).
tools.usage:
<proj>/<proj>.xpr
<proj>/<proj>.srcs/{sources_1,constrs_1,sim_1,utils_1}
<proj>/<proj>.gen/sources_1/{ip,bd}
<proj>/<proj>.runs/{synth_1,impl_1,<ip>_synth_1}
<proj>/<proj>.sim/sim_1/behav/xsim
<proj>/<proj>.cache, <proj>.hw, <proj>.ip_user_files

parameters.name: <proj>.filter
parameters.description: Binary message-suppression rules created from the Messages window.

parameters.name: Migrate to .gen
parameters.description: Projects created in 2020.1 or earlier keep outputs in .srcs until migrated (Settings > General).

tools.example:
# Revision-control friendly regeneration instead of committing .xpr + generated dirs
write_project_tcl -force -paths_relative_to ./ ./recreate_proj.tcl
# later / elsewhere
vivado -mode batch -source recreate_proj.tcl
tools.notes: Commit sources, constraints, .xci/.bd (or write_bd_tcl scripts) and the recreate script; do not commit .runs, .cache, .gen, .sim, .hw or .ip_user_files. Opening an .xpr in a newer release offers an automatic upgrade that older releases cannot open afterwards.

tools.name: Run directory files (<proj>.runs/<run>: runme.log, runme.sh/.bat, <top>.tcl, *.pb, *.rpt/*.rpx, <top>_<step>.dcp)
tools.description: What launch_runs creates in each run directory: the generated run script <top>.tcl and wrappers runme.sh/runme.bat, the run transcript runme.log, message databases (*.pb), text and interactive reports (*.rpt / *.rpx from the report strategy), a checkpoint after each step (synthesis <top>.dcp; implementation <top>_opt.dcp, _placed.dcp, _physopt.dcp, _routed.dcp), vivado.begin.rst / vivado.end.rst markers, and jobs/vrs_config_<n>.xml run definitions; write_bitstream adds <top>.bit and <top>.ltx.
tools.usage: <proj>.runs/impl_1/: runme.log, runme.sh|runme.bat, <top>.tcl, *.pb, <top>_timing_summary_routed.rpt/.rpx, <top>_utilization_placed.rpt, <top>_opt.dcp, <top>_placed.dcp, <top>_routed.dcp, <top>.bit, <top>.ltx, vivado.begin.rst, vivado.end.rst
tools.example:
# Inspect a finished run without opening the project
tail -n 30 proj.runs/impl_1/runme.log
grep -A5 'Design Timing Summary' proj.runs/impl_1/top_timing_summary_routed.rpt
vivado proj.runs/impl_1/top_routed.dcp -source analyse.tcl
# Re-run a run outside the GUI (what launch_runs does)
cd proj.runs/impl_1 && ./runme.sh
tools.notes: Do not edit files in run directories - they are regenerated on reset_run. The *.pb files feed the Messages window; the *.rst markers tell Vivado whether a run started/finished when the project is reopened.

tools.name: .xdc (Xilinx Design Constraints) and Tcl constraint files
tools.description: Text constraint files in SDC-derived Tcl syntax holding timing constraints (create_clock, set_input_delay, set_false_path...) and physical constraints (set_property PACKAGE_PIN/IOSTANDARD/LOC, Pblocks). Managed XDC files support only a Tcl subset (set, list, expr, object queries and constraint commands) and can be edited and saved back by the IDE; full Tcl (procs, loops) goes in unmanaged .tcl files added to the constraint set, which are sourced after the XDC files and never rewritten by Vivado.
tools.usage:
Project: add_files -fileset constrs_1 top.xdc
Non-project: read_xdc top.xdc  |  read_xdc -unmanaged gen.tcl  |  source gen.tcl
File properties: USED_IN_SYNTHESIS, USED_IN_IMPLEMENTATION, PROCESSING_ORDER (EARLY|NORMAL|LATE), SCOPED_TO_REF, SCOPED_TO_CELLS

parameters.name: USED_IN_SYNTHESIS / USED_IN_IMPLEMENTATION
parameters.description: Restrict a file to one flow (e.g. physical-only constraints just for implementation).

parameters.name: SCOPED_TO_REF / SCOPED_TO_CELLS
parameters.description: Apply a module-level XDC to every instance of a module or to specific cells (how IP XDCs are scoped).

parameters.name: read_xdc -unmanaged
parameters.description: Reads a Tcl constraint script while preserving its order relative to other XDCs inside the checkpoint (unlike source).

tools.example:
## top.xdc
create_clock -period 10.000 -name sys_clk [get_ports clk_100m]
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN E3 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33} [get_ports clk_100m]
set_input_delay -clock sys_clk 2.0 [get_ports {adc_d[*]}]
# Tcl
set_property USED_IN_SYNTHESIS false [get_files pblocks.xdc]
set_property PROCESSING_ORDER LATE [get_files overrides.xdc]
tools.notes: Constraints edited in the GUI go to the target constraint file only on Save Constraints; edits made to constraints originating from a Tcl file cannot be written back. UCF from ISE is not accepted and must be rewritten as XDC.

tools.name: .dcp (design checkpoint)
tools.description: Compressed archive that snapshots a design at a point in the flow: the netlist, constraints and, when available, placement and routing, so the design can be reopened for analysis or continued without rerunning earlier steps. Runs write one per step (<top>.dcp after synthesis, <top>_opt/_placed/_physopt/_routed.dcp during implementation), IP out-of-context synthesis produces one per IP, and DFX/ECO/incremental flows are built on them.
tools.usage:
write_checkpoint [-force] [-cell <cell>] <file>.dcp
open_checkpoint <file>.dcp   |  read_checkpoint [-cell <cell>] [-incremental] <file>.dcp
vivado <file>.dcp -source <script.tcl>
tools.example:
# Non-project flow with checkpoints between steps
synth_design -top top -part xc7a35tcsg324-1
write_checkpoint -force post_synth.dcp
opt_design; place_design
write_checkpoint -force post_place.dcp
route_design
write_checkpoint -force post_route.dcp
# later
open_checkpoint post_route.dcp
report_timing_summary -file ts.rpt
tools.notes: A checkpoint can be opened by the same or a newer Vivado release but not by an older one. Encrypted IP stays protected inside the DCP. Checkpoints of large devices can be hundreds of MB; keep only the ones needed (post-route for timing, post-synth for incremental).

tools.name: .xci / .xcix (IP customisation file and core container)
tools.description: The .xci (Xilinx Core Instance) file stores one IP instance's VLNV, part/board context, and all user parameter values, and is the file to add, read and revision-control for Vivado IP - Vivado regenerates output products from it. Older releases write it as IP-XACT style XML; 2022.1 and later write JSON. The optional .xcix core container is a single compressed binary holding the .xci plus all generated output products, read directly by the tools without extraction.
tools.usage:
Project: add_files ./ip/clk_wiz_0/clk_wiz_0.xci  (or clk_wiz_0.xcix)
Non-project: read_ip ./ip/clk_wiz_0/clk_wiz_0.xci; generate_target all [get_ips clk_wiz_0]
Core container: Settings > IP > Use Core Containers for IP, or right-click IP > Enable/Disable Core Container

parameters.name: coreContainer.alwaysCreateXCI
parameters.description: Project property (set_property coreContainer.alwaysCreateXCI 1 [current_project]) that keeps a plain .xci alongside the .xcix so IP changes remain diffable.

tools.example:
create_ip -name clk_wiz -vendor xilinx.com -library ip -module_name clk_wiz_0 -dir ./ip
set_property -dict [list CONFIG.CLKOUT1_REQUESTED_OUT_FREQ {200}] [get_ips clk_wiz_0]
generate_target all [get_files ./ip/clk_wiz_0/clk_wiz_0.xci]
synth_ip [get_ips clk_wiz_0]
tools.notes: Always reference IP through the .xci/.xcix, never by reading only the IP's .dcp. An .xci from an older release opens as locked until upgrade_ip is run. The 7 series Memory Interface IP and IP inside block designs cannot use core containers.

tools.name: .bd (IP Integrator block design file)
tools.description: The source file of an IP Integrator block design, stored at <proj>.srcs/sources_1/bd/<name>/<name>.bd together with a ui/ folder holding the canvas layout; since 2018.3 it is JSON (older XML .bd files convert on save). Generating the design creates per-cell IP, the HDL wrapper source, hardware handoff (.hwh) and address map data (under <proj>.gen/sources_1/bd/<name>/ in the 2020.2+ layout).
tools.usage:
create_bd_design <name>  |  open_bd_design <path>/<name>.bd  |  read_bd <path>/<name>.bd (non-project)
generate_target all [get_files <name>.bd]
make_wrapper -files [get_files <name>.bd] -top
tools.example:
read_bd ./bd/system/system.bd
set_property synth_checkpoint_mode None [get_files ./bd/system/system.bd]
generate_target all [get_files ./bd/system/system.bd]
read_verilog [make_wrapper -files [get_files ./bd/system/system.bd] -top]
tools.notes: Although JSON is diffable, the recommended revision-control artefact is the Tcl produced by write_bd_tcl, which rebuilds the design in any compatible release. A .bd opened in a newer release must be upgraded (upgrade_bd_cells) and cannot go back.

tools.name: .hwh (hardware handoff file)
tools.description: XML file generated with a block design that describes the hardware configuration: every IP cell with its VLNV and parameters, the processor configuration, address map, interrupts, clocks and resets. It is packaged into the .xsa for Vitis/PetaLinux and is read directly by PYNQ, which requires a .hwh named like the bitstream (my_overlay.bit + my_overlay.hwh).
tools.usage: <proj>.gen/sources_1/bd/<bd>/hw_handoff/<bd>.hwh   (pre-2020.2 layout: under <proj>.srcs/sources_1/bd/<bd>/hw_handoff/)
tools.example:
# Collect a PYNQ overlay after implementation
cp proj.runs/impl_1/system_wrapper.bit overlay/my_overlay.bit
cp proj.gen/sources_1/bd/system/hw_handoff/system.hwh overlay/my_overlay.hwh
# Python on the board:
# from pynq import Overlay; ol = Overlay('my_overlay.bit')
tools.notes: Regenerated whenever the block design output products are regenerated; a .hwh from a different BD revision than the bitstream gives wrong addresses in PYNQ or software. Each DFX partial bitstream needs its own .hwh for PYNQ.

tools.name: .xsa (Xilinx Support Archive) and legacy .hdf / .dsa
tools.description: The .xsa is the hardware-platform archive exported from Vivado with write_hw_platform (File > Export > Export Hardware) that Vitis, XSCT/HSI, PetaLinux and v++ consume: it bundles the hardware handoff (.hwh), processor/PS configuration and initialisation data, the address map, optionally the bitstream and .mmi, and for extensible platforms the PFM metadata. It replaced the SDK-era .hdf (write_sysdef/write_hwdef) and the SDSoC/SDAccel .dsa in the 2019.2 Vitis transition.
tools.usage:
write_hw_platform -fixed [-include_bit] [-force] -file <name>.xsa   (extensible: write_hw_platform -hw ...)
Vitis/XSCT: platform create -hw <name>.xsa  |  hsi::open_hw_design <name>.xsa
PetaLinux:  petalinux-config --get-hw-description <dir_with_xsa>

parameters.name: -fixed / -hw
parameters.description: Fixed (embedded software) platform vs. extensible platform for Vitis acceleration.

parameters.name: -include_bit
parameters.description: Put the bitstream into the archive so software tools can program the PL.

parameters.name: Legacy .hdf / .dsa
parameters.description: Vivado 2019.1 and earlier: .hdf for Xilinx SDK (write_sysdef/write_hwdef), .dsa for SDSoC/SDAccel platforms; not accepted by Vitis.

tools.example:
open_run impl_1
write_hw_platform -fixed -include_bit -force -file ./export/system_wrapper.xsa
# inspect contents (it is a zip archive)
# unzip -l ./export/system_wrapper.xsa
tools.notes: Re-export the .xsa after any hardware change and update the Vitis platform (platform config -updatehw) - stale XSAs are a common cause of wrong xparameters.h. See write_hw_platform for all options.

tools.name: .edf / .edn / .ngc (netlist formats)
tools.description: EDIF 2 0 0 netlists (.edf, commonly .edn from third-party synthesis) can be design sources, e.g. a Synplify top-level netlist or a black-box module delivered as a netlist, and write_edif exports a Vivado netlist in the same format. The ISE/XST .ngc netlist format is accepted only for 7 series designs and not for UltraScale or newer; convert with ngc2edif or, better, regenerate the IP natively.
tools.usage:
read_edif <file>.edf|.edn   |  add_files <file>.edf
write_edif [-cell <cell>] [-security_mode multifile|all] [-force] <file>.edf
write_verilog -mode synth_stub <stub>.v   (companion black-box stub)
tools.example:
# Deliver a synthesized module as netlist + stub
synth_design -top secret_core -part xcku5p-ffvb676-2-e -mode out_of_context
write_edif -force secret_core.edf
write_verilog -mode synth_stub -force secret_core_stub.v
# Consumer project
add_files {secret_core.edf secret_core_stub.v}
tools.notes: A netlist source makes the enclosing module a black box in RTL elaboration; set USED_IN properties on the stub accordingly. Encrypted IP inside a design is written to protected EDIF files depending on -security_mode.

tools.name: write_sdf
tools.description: Writes a Standard Delay Format (.sdf) file with the cell and interconnect delays of the current (usually routed) design for back-annotated timing simulation or third-party static timing analysis. It is paired with write_verilog -mode timesim -sdf_anno true, which writes the matching timing netlist.
tools.usage: write_sdf [-process_corner slow|fast] [-cell <cell>] [-rename_top <name>] [-mode timesim|sta] [-gzip] [-multithread <n>] [-force] [-quiet] [-verbose] <file>.sdf

parameters.name: -process_corner
parameters.description: slow (default) or fast delays; write one file per corner for min/max simulation.

parameters.name: -mode
parameters.description: timesim (default) for simulation or sta for static-timing tools.

parameters.name: -cell / -rename_top
parameters.description: Write a sub-hierarchy and rename its top to match the netlist written with the same options.

tools.example:
open_checkpoint top_routed.dcp
write_verilog -mode timesim -sdf_anno true -force top_timesim.v
write_sdf -process_corner slow -force top_timesim_slow.sdf
write_sdf -process_corner fast -force top_timesim_fast.sdf
# xelab ... -sdfmax /top_tb/dut=top_timesim_slow.sdf
tools.notes: Launch_simulation for post-implementation timing simulation generates both files automatically. Timing simulation is slow; use static timing (report_timing_summary) for sign-off and SDF simulation only for specific checks.

tools.name: .saif / .vcd (switching activity and value-change dump files)
tools.description: SAIF (Switching Activity Interchange Format) records per-net toggle counts and signal probabilities from simulation and is the file Vivado's power analysis reads (read_saif) to replace vectorless estimates. VCD (Value Change Dump, IEEE 1364) records every value change with time and is used for waveform exchange with other viewers and for exporting ILA captures.
tools.usage:
SAIF from XSim: open_saif act.saif; log_saif [get_objects -r /tb/dut/*]; run 100us; close_saif
Power: read_saif -strip_path tb/dut act.saif; report_power
VCD from XSim: open_vcd dump.vcd; log_vcd [get_objects -r /tb/*]; run all; close_vcd
VCD from ILA: write_hw_ila_data -vcd_file capture.vcd [upload_hw_ila_data [get_hw_ilas hw_ila_1]]
tools.example:
# Post-implementation functional sim producing SAIF for accurate power
open_saif top_activity.saif
log_saif [get_objects -r /tb_top/dut/*]
run 200us
close_saif
# in the implemented design
read_saif -strip_path tb_top/dut top_activity.saif
report_power -file power_saif.rpt
tools.notes: SAIF from post-implementation simulation matches netlist names best; with RTL SAIF many nets remain unmatched (check the read_saif match summary). Large VCDs grow quickly - log only the scopes needed.

tools.name: .mmi / .mem / .elf (memory-initialisation files)
tools.description: Files for putting software or data into block RAM: .elf is the executable from Vitis/GCC for a MicroBlaze or other soft processor; .mmi (Memory Map Information, XML) from write_mem_info describes which BRAM sites hold which address ranges of each processor or XPM memory; .mem is an ASCII hex format with optional @address lines used by updatemem -data, by XPM memories' MEMORY_INIT_FILE and by $readmemh in simulation.
tools.usage:
write_mem_info -force design.mmi
updatemem -meminfo design.mmi -data app.elf|data.mem -proc <cell_path> -bit in.bit -out out.bit
XPM: xpm_memory_spram #(.MEMORY_INIT_FILE("init.mem"), ...)
.mem syntax: @0000 00000013 00000093 ... (hex words)
tools.example:
# init.mem
@0000
DEADBEEF 00000001 00000002 00000003
@0010
CAFEF00D
# Tcl
write_mem_info -force top.mmi
exec updatemem -meminfo top.mmi -data sw/app.elf -proc design_1_i/microblaze_0 -bit top.bit -out top_app.bit -force
tools.notes: The .mmi must come from the same implementation as the .bit. For in-project ELF merging use Tools > Associate ELF Files instead. The legacy .bmm format (write_bmm) served the same role as .mmi for data2mem.

tools.name: .coe / .mif (coefficient and memory-initialisation files for IP)
tools.description: The .coe file is a small text format used to initialise Block Memory Generator and Distributed Memory Generator contents (memory_initialization_radix / memory_initialization_vector) and to load FIR Compiler coefficients (radix / coefdata). When the IP is generated Vivado converts the .coe into a .mif (one binary word per line) used by the IP's simulation model.
tools.example:
set_property -dict [list CONFIG.Load_Init_File {true} CONFIG.Coe_File {/work/rom/sine.coe}] [get_ips sine_rom]
generate_target all [get_ips sine_rom]
# FIR
set_property -dict [list CONFIG.CoefficientSource {COE_File} CONFIG.Coefficient_File {/work/fir/lpf.coe}] [get_ips fir_lpf]
tools.notes: Vectors are separated by commas or whitespace and the list ends with a semicolon; the number of entries must not exceed the memory depth. Keep .coe files beside the .xci under revision control and use absolute or project-relative paths that exist on every build machine.

tools.name: read_csv / write_csv (.csv I/O pin planning files)
tools.description: Import and export I/O port and package-pin information as CSV, the standard exchange format with PCB designers: write_csv dumps package pins with the ports placed on them and their I/O properties, and read_csv creates or updates ports from a CSV in an I/O Planning project (port name, direction, pin, I/O standard, drive, slew, diff-pair and interface columns).
tools.usage:
write_csv [-force] [-quiet] [-verbose] <file>.csv
read_csv [-quiet_diff_pairs] [-quiet] [-verbose] <file>.csv
GUI: I/O Ports window > Export I/O Ports (CSV/XDC/Verilog/VHDL); File > Import > Import I/O Ports

parameters.name: -quiet_diff_pairs
parameters.description: Suppress messages about differential pairs inferred while importing.

parameters.name: -force
parameters.description: Overwrite an existing CSV.

tools.example:
# Start a pin plan from the board team's CSV
create_project -part xc7k325tffg900-2 pinplan ./pinplan
set_property design_mode PinPlanning [current_fileset]
open_io_design -name io_1
read_csv ./board/fpga_pins.csv
report_io -file io_after_import.rpt
report_drc -file drc_after_import.rpt
write_csv -force ./board/fpga_pins_checked.csv
tools.notes: CSV import is intended for I/O Planning projects; for RTL projects ports come from the HDL and placement is exchanged via XDC. Run report_io / report_drc after every import because the CSV can contain illegal standards or banks.

tools.name: write_ibis (.ibs IBIS models)
tools.description: Writes an IBIS model file for the current design's I/O configuration (the I/O standards, drive, slew and termination actually used on each pin), which board designers use for signal-integrity simulation. Package parasitics can be written per pin and model selection limited to used standards unless -allmodels is given.
tools.usage: write_ibis [-force] [-allmodels] [-nopin] [-no_pin_mapping] [-truncate <n>] [-ibs <model_file>] [-pkg <package_file>] [-component_name <name>] [-quiet] [-verbose] <file>.ibs

parameters.name: -allmodels
parameters.description: Include all buffer models of the device, not only those used by the design.

parameters.name: -nopin
parameters.description: Omit per-pin package parasitics from the [Pin] section.

parameters.name: -truncate
parameters.description: Limit signal-name length for tools with name-length limits.

parameters.name: -component_name
parameters.description: Name of the [Component] in the file.

tools.example:
open_run impl_1
write_ibis -force -component_name fpga_u1 ./si/fpga_u1.ibs
tools.notes: Generate the IBIS file from the final implemented (or at least pin-locked) design so standards and terminations match the board. Generic per-device IBIS files are also downloadable from AMD for early SI work.

tools.name: .ucf (legacy ISE constraints)
tools.description: The User Constraints File format of ISE (NET/INST/TIMESPEC statements) is not supported by Vivado. Designs migrated from ISE must have their timing and physical constraints rewritten as XDC, using the ISE to Vivado migration guide's mapping (e.g. NET "clk" LOC = "E3" becomes set_property PACKAGE_PIN E3 [get_ports clk]).
tools.example:
# Typical conversions
# NET "rst_n" TIG;                -> set_false_path -from [get_ports rst_n]
# INST "u_sync/*" TNM = sync_grp; -> use get_cells u_sync/* in XDC commands
# OFFSET = IN 2 ns BEFORE clk;     -> set_input_delay -clock sys_clk [expr 10.0 - 2.0] [get_ports din*]
tools.notes: OFFSET constraints do not map 1:1 - recompute input/output delays from the board timing. Vivado supports only 7 series and newer devices, so projects for Spartan-6 and older must stay in ISE.

tools.name: .nky (bitstream encryption key file)
tools.description: Text file holding the AES-256 key (and related values) used to encrypt a 7 series or UltraScale(+) bitstream. It is either supplied through BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.KEYFILE or generated by write_bitstream when encryption is enabled, and the same file is used in the Hardware Manager to program the key into the device's battery-backed RAM or eFUSEs.
tools.usage:
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPT YES [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPTKEYSELECT BBRAM|eFUSE [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.KEYFILE ./keys/prod.nky [current_design]   (or BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.KEY0 <hex>)
Hardware Manager: right-click device > Program BBR Key... / Program eFUSE Registers...
tools.example:
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPT YES [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPTKEYSELECT BBRAM [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.KEYFILE /secure/keys/prod.nky [current_design]
write_bitstream -force top_enc.bit
tools.notes: Treat .nky files as secrets: keep them out of the project tree and revision control. eFUSE programming is irreversible. Zynq/MPSoC/Versal boot images handle keys through bootgen (.nky/.bif attributes) instead.

tools.name: Vivado part names, speed grades and temperature grades
tools.description: Vivado part names differ from ordering codes. 7 series parts join device and package, then speed grade (xc7a35tcsg324-1; ordering code XC7A35T-1CSG324C), with low-voltage industrial variants marked by 'i' and an L grade (xc7a35ticsg324-1L). UltraScale and UltraScale+ use device-package-speed-temperature (xczu9eg-ffvb1156-2-e, xcvu9p-flga2104-2L-e), and Versal adds voltage/power letters to the speed grade plus a suffix (xcvc1902-vsva2197-2MP-e-S).
tools.usage:
Speed grade: -1 (slowest), -2, -3 (fastest); L / LV / LE variants run at reduced core voltage (e.g. -1L, -2LE, -2LV).
Temperature grade: C 0..85 C, E 0..100 C, I -40..100 C, Q -40..125 C, M -55..125 C (Tj).
Prefix: XC commercial/industrial, XA automotive, XQ defense-grade.
Versal speed grades carry a voltage letter - L (0.70 V), M (0.80 V), H (0.88 V) - as in -2MP; ordering codes additionally mark static-power screening (S standard, L low).

parameters.name: Package code
parameters.description: Letters+pin count, e.g. csg324, ffg900, ffvb1156, sfvc784, vsva2197; the ball pitch and lid type are encoded in the letters.

parameters.name: Board part vs part
parameters.description: Setting BOARD_PART selects the part automatically; the part alone carries no board pin-out.

tools.example:
get_parts -filter {DEVICE == xczu9eg && SPEED == -2}
report_property [get_parts xczu9eg-ffvb1156-2-e]
create_project p1 ./p1 -part xc7a100tcsg324-1
set_property part xczu3eg-sbva484-1-e [current_project]
tools.notes: Timing models differ per speed grade (and per voltage for L/LV grades), so the part in the project must match the soldered device; temperature grade does not change the part name for 7 series but does for UltraScale and newer. Engineering-sample parts may carry extra suffixes (e.g. -es1) and need separate enablement.

tools.name: 7 series FPGAs and SoCs (Spartan-7, Artix-7, Kintex-7, Virtex-7, Zynq-7000)
tools.description: The oldest family generation supported by Vivado (28 nm): Spartan-7 (xc7s, cost-optimised, no transceivers), Artix-7 (xc7a, low-cost with GTP transceivers), Kintex-7 (xc7k, mid-range with GTX), Virtex-7 (xc7v/xc7vx/xc7vh, high-end with GTX/GTH/GTZ) and Zynq-7000 SoC (xc7z, dual/single Cortex-A9 PS plus 7 series PL). Primitives include MMCME2/PLLE2, DSP48E1, RAMB18E1/RAMB36E1, BUFG/BUFH/BUFR/BUFIO clocking and ISERDESE2/OSERDESE2 I/O.
tools.usage:
Parts: xc7s50csga324-1, xc7a35tcsg324-1, xc7k325tffg900-2, xc7vx485tffg1761-2, xc7z020clg400-1
Architecture property names: spartan7, artix7, kintex7, virtex7, zynq
tools.example:
get_parts -filter {ARCHITECTURE == artix7 && SPEED == -1} xc7a35t*
create_project a7 ./a7 -part xc7a35tcsg324-1
# Zynq-7000 embedded: processing_system7 IP in a block design, boot image via bootgen -arch zynq
tools.notes: Standard (free) edition covers all Spartan-7, Artix-7 up to XC7A200T, Kintex-7 XC7K70T/160T and Zynq-7000 up to XC7Z030 plus the single-core S devices (per UG973 2022.2); larger Kintex-7, all Virtex-7 and bigger Zynq need Enterprise. Spartan-6 and older families require ISE.

tools.name: UltraScale and UltraScale+ families (Kintex/Virtex UltraScale(+), Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC/RFSoC, Artix UltraScale+)
tools.description: UltraScale (20 nm): Kintex UltraScale (xcku025-xcku115) and Virtex UltraScale (xcvu065-xcvu440). UltraScale+ (16 nm): Kintex UltraScale+ (xcku*p), Virtex UltraScale+ (xcvu*p, including HBM and 58G variants), Artix UltraScale+ (xcau*p), Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC (xczu*cg/eg/ev with Cortex-A53/R5F PS, GPU in EG/EV, video codec in EV) and Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC (xczu*dr with RF data converters). Common primitives: MMCME4/PLLE4, DSP48E2, RAMB36E2, UltraRAM (URAM288, UltraScale+), BUFGCE/BUFG_GT, GTH/GTY transceivers; large Virtex parts are multi-SLR (SSI) devices.
tools.usage:
Parts: xcku040-ffva1156-2-e, xcku5p-ffvb676-2-e, xcvu9p-flga2104-2L-e, xcau15p-ffvb676-2-e, xczu9eg-ffvb1156-2-e, xczu28dr-ffvg1517-2-e
Architecture property examples: kintexu, virtexu, kintexuplus, virtexuplus, zynquplus
tools.example:
get_parts -filter {ARCHITECTURE == zynquplus} xczu3eg*
create_project zu ./zu -part xczu3eg-sbva484-1-e
get_slrs   ;# >1 on SSI devices such as xcvu9p
tools.notes: Per UG973 2022.2 the free Standard edition includes Kintex UltraScale KU025/KU035, Kintex UltraScale+ KU3P/KU5P, Artix UltraScale+ AU10P-AU25P and Zynq UltraScale+ ZU1-ZU5 plus ZU7 variants; Virtex, RFSoC and the rest need Enterprise. Check the release notes of the version in use, as the lists change.

tools.name: Versal adaptive SoCs (Prime, AI Core, AI Edge, Premium, HBM series)
tools.description: 7 nm adaptive SoC family combining a processing system (Cortex-A72 and Cortex-R5F), the Platform Management Controller (PMC), programmable logic, a hardened Network on Chip and, in AI series, AI Engine arrays. Series: Prime (xcvm), AI Core (xcvc), AI Edge (xcve), Premium (xcvp) and HBM (xcvh), with newer RF and Gen 2 series added in later releases. Designs are built around the CIPS and AXI NoC IP, and the programmable output is a PDI written by write_device_image rather than a .bit.
tools.usage:
Parts: xcvc1902-vsva2197-2MP-e-S (VCK190), xcvm1802-vsva2197-2MP-e-S, xcve2802-vsvh1760-2MP-e-S (VEK280)
Flow: block design with versal_cips + axi_noc -> implementation -> write_device_image top.pdi -> bootgen -arch versal / Vitis platform
tools.example:
create_project v ./v -part xcvc1902-vsva2197-2MP-e-S
# ... block design with versal_cips, axi_noc ...
launch_runs impl_1 -to_step write_device_image -jobs 8
wait_on_run impl_1
tools.notes: Versal debug uses cs_server in addition to hw_server. Versal devices were not in the Standard edition in 2022.2; later releases changed edition coverage, so check UG973 for the version in use. AI Engine programming is done in Vitis (aiecompiler), not Vivado.

tools.name: Spartan UltraScale+ FPGAs
tools.description: Cost-optimised, I/O-rich 16 nm FPGA family (xcsu*p) aimed at sensor/control, board-management and edge applications that previously used Spartan-7 or Artix-7. The first devices, XCSU10P, XCSU25P and XCSU35P, reached production status with Vivado 2025.1; larger family members follow in later releases.
tools.usage: Select in the New Project wizard part list or with get_parts xcsu* (requires Vivado 2025.1 or later with the Spartan UltraScale+ device family installed).
tools.example:
get_parts xcsu35p*
# create_project su ./su -part <one of the listed xcsu35p parts>
tools.notes: Confirm package names and production status in the release notes of the version you install; engineering-sample devices appear only when the corresponding device support is enabled. Being UltraScale+-based, it uses UltraScale+-generation primitives and design methodology rather than 7 series ones.

tools.name: Kria SOMs (K26, K24) and starter kits (KV260, KR260, KD240)
tools.description: Production system-on-modules built on custom Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC devices: the K26 (XCK26, EV-class with video codec, -2LV speed grade) used on the KV260 Vision AI and KR260 Robotics starter kits, and the smaller K24 (XCK24) used on the KD240 Drives starter kit. In Vivado they are targeted through board parts from the Vivado Store (e.g. kv260_som / kr260_som, with the carrier-card connection) or by part name, and Kria targets are covered by the free ML Standard Edition.
tools.usage:
Board: install the SOM/carrier board files (Tools > Vivado Store > Boards, or xhub::install), then create_project ... ; set_property board_part xilinx.com:kv260_som:part0:<ver> [current_project]
Part only: create_project k26 ./k26 -part xck26-sfvc784-2LV-c   (industrial: -2LV-i)
tools.example:
xhub::refresh_catalog [xhub::get_xstores xilinx_board_store]
xhub::install [xhub::get_xitems *kv260*]
create_project kv260_hw ./kv260_hw
set_property board_part [lindex [get_board_parts *kv260_som*] end] [current_project]
# block design with zynq_ultra_ps_e + apply_bd_automation using the board preset
tools.notes: Kria software typically loads PL designs at runtime as 'accelerated applications' (bitstream + device-tree overlay via xmutil/dfx-mgr) rather than from BOOT.BIN. The XCK26 part may not appear in the GUI part list like ordinary Zynq UltraScale+ parts; select it via the board part or by the exact part name in Tcl.
